name: Monarchists and Octobrists
sum: The old right. In Reed’s ten days they no longer act in their own name; their men work through the Cadets and the generals.

def.q: These once-powerful factions no longer existed openly; they either worked underground, or their members joined the Cadets, as the Cadets came by degrees to stand for their political programme.

background.en: The Octobrists, the Union of 17 October, took their name from the Tsar’s manifesto of October 1905 that promised a constitution, and were the largest party of the Third Duma. Mikhail Rodzianko, an Octobrist, chaired the Duma from 1911 until 1917; Vasily Shulgin led the Duma’s Russian nationalists. After the February Revolution the monarchist right lost its place in open politics.

name: Cadets (Constitutional Democrats)
sum: The liberal party of the propertied and the professions: its men sit in the last Kerensky cabinet, the Council of the Republic and the City Duma, and fight the rising from them.

def.q: So-called from the initials of its name, Constitutional Democrats. Its official name is “Party of the People’s Freedom.”

also.q: As the Revolution became more and more a social economic Revolution, the Cadets grew more and more conservative.

background.en: Founded in 1905 and led by the historian Pavel Miliukov, the party of liberal lawyers, professors and zemstvo men stood for a constitutional state, civil rights and, in 1917, a republic that would fight the war to victory. Its leaders formed most of the first Provisional Government. On 11 December 1917 the Soviet government declared it a party of “enemies of the people” and arrested its leaders.

name: Group of Public Men
sum: Moscow’s bankers and manufacturers: their delegates hold portfolios in Kerensky’s last cabinet, Konovalov among them.

def.q: After the Cadets had become unpopular through their relations with the Kornilov counter-revolution, the Group of Public Men was formed in Moscow.

also.q: It was composed of the more “modern” bankers, merchants and manufacturers, who were intelligent enough to realise that the Soviets must be fought by their own weapon—economic organisation.

background.en: The Conference of Public Figures met in Moscow in August 1917, on the eve of General Kornilov’s attempt on Petrograd, with Mikhail Rodzianko in the chair; it brought together industrialists, bankers, landowners and conservative politicians who wanted a strong government against the Soviets. Alexander Konovalov, a textile magnate, was deputy prime minister in Kerensky’s last cabinet.

name: Populist Socialists (Trudoviki)
sum: A small, cautious socialist party of the cooperatives; it stands with the Government and the Duma against the rising.

def.q: Numerically a small party, composed of cautious intellectuals, the leaders of the Cooperative societies, and conservative peasants.

also.q: Kerensky was the leader of the Trudoviki in the Imperial Duma when the Revolution of March, 1917, broke out.

background.en: The Popular Socialists broke away from the Socialist Revolutionaries’ right in 1906, rejecting terror and the immediate socialisation of the land; in June 1917 they merged with the Trudoviks, the peasant Labour Group of the Imperial Duma, as the Labour Popular Socialist Party. Aleksey Peshekhonov was minister of food in 1917, and Nikolai Tchaikovsky, a veteran of the 1870s, led the Cooperative movement.

name: Russian Social Democratic Labour Party
sum: Russia’s Marxist party, long split: by 1917 its wings, from the Bolsheviki to Plekhanov’s Yedinstvo, are parties of their own, on both sides of the barricades.

def.q: At a party congress held in 1903, the party split, on the question of tactics, into two factions—the Majority (Bolshinstvo), and the Minority (Menshinstvo).

also.q: These two wings became two separate parties, both calling themselves “Russian Social Democratic Labour Party,” and both professing to be Marxians.

background.en: Founded at Minsk in 1898. At its Second Congress, in Brussels and London in 1903, Lenin’s followers and Martov’s split over who should be a member of the party: Lenin wanted a tight body of professional revolutionaries, Martov a broader party. The two wings, Bolsheviks and Mensheviks, were separate parties by 1912.

name: Mensheviki (Mensheviks)
sum: The moderate Marxists, in coalition with the Cadets since May; they walk out of the Congress of Soviets and join the Committee for Salvation.

def.q: This party includes all shades of Socialists who believe that society must progress by natural evolution toward Socialism, and that the working-class must conquer political power first.

also.q: This was the party of the Socialist intellectuals

background.en: The Mensheviks held that backward Russia was ready only for a bourgeois, democratic revolution, which the workers should push forward but not lead to socialism at once. In 1917 the “defencists” among them, led by Irakli Tsereteli, Fyodor Dan and Nikolay Chkheidze, dominated the Soviets until September, entered the coalition government in May and backed the defence of the country in the war.

name: Menshevik Internationalists
sum: Martov’s left Mensheviks: against the war and the coalition, and against the rising too; they leave the Congress, then work for a government of all the socialist parties.

def.q: The radical wing of the Mensheviki, internationalists and opposed to all coalition with the propertied classes; yet unwilling to break loose from the conservative Mensheviki, and opposed to the dictatorship of the working-class advocated by the Bolsheviki.

also.q: Trotzky was long a member of this group.

background.en: Martov’s internationalists opposed the war from 1914 and the coalition with the Cadets in 1917. At the opening of the Second Congress of Soviets Martov proposed a peaceful settlement and a government of all the socialist parties; when the Congress endorsed the rising he walked out, and Trotsky told him to go where he belonged, into the dustbin of history.

name: Bolsheviki (Bolsheviks)
sum: Lenin’s party, with the majority in the Petrograd Soviet: it makes the rising through the Military Revolutionary Committee and forms the Council of People’s Commissars.

def.q: The Bolsheviki proposed immediate proletarian insurrection, and seizure of the reins of Government, in order to hasten the coming of Socialism by forcibly taking over industry, land, natural resources and financial institutions.

also.q: This party expresses the desires chiefly of the factory workers, but also of a large section of the poor peasants.

background.en: From April 1917 Lenin’s Bolsheviks called for “All power to the Soviets”, for peace and for land. They won the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets in September, prepared the rising through the Petrograd Soviet’s Military Revolutionary Committee, and on 8 November formed the Council of People’s Commissars. In March 1918 the party renamed itself the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks).

name: Novaya Zhizn group (United Social Democrats Internationalists)
sum: Gorky’s paper and its circle: they condemn the rising, yet stay in the Congress and plead for a socialist coalition.

def.q: Also called the Novaya Zhizn (New Life) group, from the name of the very influential newspaper which was its organ.

also.q: Opposed the Bolshevik tactics, but remained in the Soviet Government.

background.en: Novaya Zhizn (“New Life”), the daily Maxim Gorky founded in Petrograd in April 1917 with Nikolai Sukhanov and others, attacked both the coalition government and the Bolsheviks; in its columns Gorky called the rising a reckless experiment on the Russian people. The Soviet government closed it in July 1918.

name: Yedinstvo
sum: Plekhanov’s following: for the war and against the rising.

def.q: A very small and dwindling group, composed almost entirely of the personal following of Plekhanov, one of the pioneers of the Russian Social Democratic movement in the 80’s, and its greatest theoretician.

background.en: Georgi Plekhanov, who brought Marxism to Russia in the 1880s, came home from exile in 1917; his group, named after its paper Yedinstvo (“Unity”), backed the war to victory and the Provisional Government, and condemned the October rising. Plekhanov died in Finland in May 1918.

name: The Bund (Jewish Social Democrats)
sum: The Jewish socialist workers’ party; it sides with the Mensheviki and walks out of the Congress with them.

def.q: Then came Abramovitch, for the Bund, the organ of the Jewish Social Democrats

background.en: The General Jewish Labour Bund of Lithuania, Poland and Russia, founded in Vilna in 1897, organised Jewish workers and stood for their national-cultural autonomy within a socialist Russia. In 1917 it sided with the Mensheviks, and its leaders, among them Mark Liber and Raphael Abramovitch, were also Menshevik leaders.

name: Socialist Revolutionaries (SRs)
sum: Russia’s largest party, the peasants’ party: Kerensky and Avksentiev are of it; it leads the Committee for Salvation and the yunker rising.

def.q: Originally the revolutionary party of the peasants, the party of the Fighting Organisations—the Terrorists.

also.q: They finally came to represent the wealthier peasants, the intellectuals, and the politically uneducated populations of remote rural districts.

background.en: Founded in 1902 as heirs of the nineteenth-century Populists, the SRs wanted the land for those who work it, and their Combat Organisation assassinated ministers. In 1917 they were Russia’s largest party: Kerensky and Viktor Chernov sat in the Provisional Government, and in the elections to the Constituent Assembly, held in late November 1917, the SRs won the most votes.

name: Left Socialist Revolutionaries
sum: The SRs’ left wing: they stay in the Congress, back the Soviet power, win the Peasants’ Congress, and join the Council of People’s Commissars.

def.q: Although theoretically sharing the Bolshevik programme of dictatorship of the working-class, at first were reluctant to follow the ruthless Bolshevik tactics.

also.q: which became the great peasant party supporting the Soviet Government, standing for confiscation without compensation of the great landed estates, and their disposition by the peasants themselves.

background.en: The SR left, led by Maria Spiridonova, Boris Kamkov and Mark Natanson, stayed in the Second Congress when the rest of the party walked out, was expelled by the SRs and founded its own party in December 1917. Its members joined the Council of People’s Commissars that month, Andrei Kolegaev as Commissar of Agriculture, and left it in March 1918 over the peace of Brest-Litovsk; their rising in Moscow in July 1918 ended the alliance with the Bolsheviks.

name: Maximalists
sum: A handful of peasant anarchists on the Soviet side.

def.q: An off-shoot of the Socialist Revolutionary party in the Revolution of 1905, when it was a powerful peasant movement, demanding the immediate application of the maximum Socialist programme.

background.en: The Union of SR Maximalists broke away from the SRs in 1904–1906, demanding that the land and the factories be socialised at once, and practised expropriation and terror. In 1917 the little group supported the Soviet seizure of power.

name: Soviets
sum: The councils of workers’, soldiers’ and peasants’ deputies, in whose name the rising is made: “All Power to the Soviets!”

def.q: The word soviet means “council.”

also.q: the term Soviet has come to be associated with a certain type of parliament elected by members of working-class economic organisations—the Soviet of Workers’, of Soldiers’, or of Peasants’ Deputies.

background.en: Workers’ councils first appeared in the revolution of 1905, when Trotsky chaired the St Petersburg Soviet. Revived in February 1917, they shared power with the Provisional Government, the “dual power”, until the Second All-Russian Congress of Soviets declared itself the government on 7–8 November.

name: Petrograd Soviet
ru: Петроградский Совет рабочих и солдатских депутатов
sum: The capital’s council of workers’ and soldiers’ deputies, Bolshevik since September, with Trotzky in the chair: its Military Revolutionary Committee makes the rising.

def.q: On the 29th, in open session of the Petrograd Soviet, Trotzky proposed that the Soviet formally sanction the Military Revolutionary Committee.

background.en: Formed on 12 March 1917 in the Tauride Palace by workers’ and soldiers’ deputies, it ran the city alongside the Provisional Government. It passed to the Bolsheviks in September 1917, when Trotsky became its chairman, and in October it set up the Military Revolutionary Committee that made the rising. It sat at Smolny.

name: Second All-Russian Congress of Soviets
sum: The congress that opens at Smolny on the night of the rising; after the Mensheviki and SRs walk out it takes power, decrees peace and land, and names the Council of People’s Commissars.

def.q: It was 10.40 P. M. Dan, a mild-faced, baldish figure in a shapeless military surgeon’s uniform, was ringing the bell.

background.en: It opened in the great hall of Smolny late on 7 November with the Bolsheviks the largest group and the Left SRs their allies. Through the night the Mensheviks, the SRs and the Bund walked out; the rest proclaimed the power of the Soviets, and on 8 November passed the decrees on peace and on land, elected the Council of People’s Commissars and chose a new Central Executive Committee.

name: The old Tsay-ee-kah (Central Executive Committee)
sum: The executive the first Congress of Soviets elected in June, moderate socialist: it tries to put off the Second Congress, then refuses to recognise it.

def.q: All-Russian Central Executive Committee of the Soviets of Workers’ and Soldiers’ Deputies. So called from the initials of its name.

background.en: Elected by the First Congress of Soviets in June 1917 with a Menshevik and SR majority under Nikolay Chkheidze, it backed the coalition government and wanted the Second Congress postponed. Its leaders denied the Congress’s authority and joined the Committee for Salvation.

name: The new Tsay-ee-kah
sum: The executive the Second Congress elects, Bolshevik with the Left SRs: Kameniev chairs it, then Sverdlov; the peasants’ deputies join it later in November.

def.q: Kameniev was stripped of his powers as president of the Tsay-ee-kah, and Sverdlov elected in his place.

background.en: Elected by the Second Congress of Soviets on 9 November 1917, with a Bolshevik majority and Left SRs, it was the Soviet state’s standing legislature between congresses. Lev Kamenev chaired it until 21 November, when Yakov Sverdlov replaced him; later that month it merged with the executive of the Peasants’ Congress.

name: Executive Committee of the Peasants’ Soviets
names: Executive Committee of the Peasants’ Soviets
ru: Исполнительный комитет Всероссийского Совета крестьянских депутатов
sum: The peasants’ executive, SR-led: it condemns the rising and joins the Committee for Salvation.

def.q: with an Executive Committee of the All-Russian Peasants’ Soviets in the capital.

background.en: Elected by the First All-Russian Congress of Peasants’ Deputies in May 1917, with an SR majority and Nikolai Avksentiev as its chairman, it stood with the Provisional Government and refused to recognise the Council of People’s Commissars.

name: Extraordinary Congress of Peasants’ Soviets
ru: Чрезвычайный Всероссийский съезд Советов крестьянских депутатов
sum: The peasant deputies who gather in Petrograd from late November: its Left SR majority, under Spiridonova, joins the Soviet power, and its SR minority walks out.

def.q: The Soviets of Peasants’ Deputies did not join the other two until after the Bolshevik coup d’etat.

background.en: The Extraordinary Congress of Peasants’ Deputies opened in Petrograd on 23 November 1917 and chose Maria Spiridonova to chair it; its Left SR majority agreed to merge with the workers’ and soldiers’ Central Executive Committee, and the Right SR minority left.

name: Military Revolutionary Committee
sum: The Petrograd Soviet’s committee that commands the garrison and the Red Guards, takes the city on 6–7 November, and holds it for the Soviets.

def.q: We ought,” he said, “to create our special organisation to march to battle, and if necessary to die….”

also.q: On the 29th, in open session of the Petrograd Soviet, Trotzky proposed that the Soviet formally sanction the Military Revolutionary Committee.

background.en: Set up by the Petrograd Soviet in October 1917, formally to defend the capital, it was the general staff of the rising. Its chairman was the Left SR Pavel Lazimir, its work was run by Bolsheviks such as Nikolai Podvoisky and Vladimir Antonov-Ovseenko under Trotsky’s lead, and it sent commissars into every unit of the garrison. It governed the city for weeks after the rising.

name: Council of People’s Commissars
sum: The Soviet government the Congress names on 8 November, with Lenin at its head.

def.q: The governmental power is vested in a collegium made up of the chairmen of these commissions, that is to say, the Council of People’s Commissars.

background.en: The government elected by the Second Congress of Soviets on 8 November 1917: at first all Bolsheviks, with Lenin as chairman, Trotsky for foreign affairs, Lunacharsky for education, and Antonov-Ovseenko, Krylenko and Dybenko for the army and navy. The Left SRs joined it in December 1917.

name: Factory-Shop Committees
sum: The workers’ committees in the mills and works, behind the Bolsheviki.

def.q: These were spontaneous organisations created in the factories by the workers in their attempt to control industry, taking advantage of the administrative break-down incident upon the Revolution.

background.en: Elected in the works from March 1917, the factory committees pressed for workers’ control of production and were Bolshevik strongholds before the Soviets were. The Soviet decree on workers’ control of 27 November 1917 gave them legal powers.

name: Trade Unions
sum: Millions of workers in industrial unions, divided over the rising.

def.q: Although mostly industrial in form, the Russian labour unions were still called Trade Unions, and at the time of the Bolshevik Revolution had from three to four million members.

background.en: The unions’ All-Russian Central Council was set up at a conference in June 1917. In November the unions were split over the Soviet power: the metalworkers backed it, the printers and the railwaymen’s leaders opposed it or demanded a coalition of all the socialist parties.

name: Vikzhel (Railway Workers’ Union)
sum: The railwaymen’s executive, neutral and powerful: it will not move troops for either side and demands a government of all the socialist parties.

def.q: All-Russian Central Committee of the Railway Workers’ Union. So called from the initials of its name.

also.q: In the name of the strongest organisation in Russia I demand the right to speak

background.en: Led by Mensheviks and SRs, the railwaymen’s executive declared itself neutral after the rising and threatened a general rail strike unless a government of all the socialist parties was formed. It called the talks on such a coalition in November 1917; they failed within days.

name: Army Committees
sum: The soldiers’ elected committees, from the company up: the higher ones stand by the old leaders, the lower ones by the Soviets.

def.q: The Army Committees were formed by the soldiers at the front to combat the reactionary influence of the old regime officers.

background.en: Soldiers’ committees spread through the army after the Petrograd Soviet’s Order No. 1 of 14 March 1917. Those elected in the spring were mostly SR and Menshevik at the higher levels, while by the autumn the regimental committees were turning Bolshevik; the Central Army Committee at Headquarters opposed the rising.

name: Fleet Committees and Tsentroflot
sum: The sailors’ committees: the Baltic sailors are the rising’s shock troops; the navy’s central committee, Tsentroflot, stands aside.

def.q: The corresponding organisations in the Navy.

background.en: Tsentrobalt, the Baltic Fleet’s central committee, chaired from April 1917 by the sailor Pavel Dybenko, refused to obey the Provisional Government in the autumn and sent the Kronstadt and Helsingfors sailors to Petrograd for the rising. Tsentroflot, the navy’s all-Russian committee, was pushed aside by the Bolsheviks after it.

name: Provisional Government
sum: Kerensky’s coalition cabinet, besieged in the Winter Palace on 7 November and arrested there that night.

def.q: When the Revolution broke out in March, 1917, the Cadets formed the first Provisional Government.

background.en: Formed by leaders of the Duma on 15 March 1917, after the Tsar abdicated, under Prince Lvov and from July under Kerensky. It governed in coalition with the moderate socialists from May, kept Russia in the war, and put off the land question and the Constituent Assembly. Its last ministers were arrested in the Winter Palace in the early hours of 8 November.

name: Council of the Republic (the Pre-Parliament)
sum: The consultative parliament in the Mariinsky Palace, dispersed by sailors on 7 November.

def.q: a sort of consultative Parliament, without any legislative power, called the Provisional Council of the Russian Republic.

background.en: Set up by the Democratic Conference and opened on 20 October 1917 in the Mariinsky Palace, with Nikolai Avksentiev as its president; the Bolsheviks walked out on its first day. Soldiers and sailors of the Military Revolutionary Committee dispersed it on 7 November.

name: City Duma
sum: Petrograd’s elected town council, under the SR mayor Schreider: the heart of the resistance in the first days, where the Committee for Salvation is born.

def.q: The City Duma referred to in this book was the reorganised Municipal Council, often called “Municipal Self-Government.”

background.en: Elected by universal suffrage in August 1917, with the SRs the largest party, the Petrograd City Duma chose Grigory Schreider as mayor. After the rising it became a centre of resistance to the Soviet power, and the Council of People’s Commissars dissolved it at the end of November 1917.

name: Committee for Salvation of Country and Revolution
sum: The coalition of everyone against the rising, formed in the City Duma on its first night; it plans the yunker rising of 11 November.

def.q: the Committee for Salvation was formed—that Committee which was to develop into the most powerful enemy of the Bolsheviki

background.en: Founded in the City Duma on the night of 7–8 November 1917 by the Duma, the old Central Executive Committee, the Peasants’ Executive, the Mensheviks, the SRs and others who had left the Congress of Soviets. It called for resistance, organised the rising of the yunkers on 11 November, and broke up after its failure.

name: Union of Unions
sum: The professional men’s federation; in 1917 it backs the officials’ strike against the Soviets.

def.q: In 1905 the Union of Unions acted with the revolutionary democracy; in 1917, however, the Union of Unions opposed the Bolshevik uprising, and united the Government employees who went on strike against the authority of the Soviets.

background.en: Formed in May 1905 by the new unions of lawyers, doctors, engineers, teachers and other professions, with Pavel Miliukov as its chairman, it backed the general strike of October 1905.

name: Zemstvos
sum: The county councils of the countryside.

def.q: May be roughly translated “county councils.”

background.en: The elected rural self-government created by Alexander II’s reform of 1864. In the war their All-Russian Union, under Prince Georgy Lvov, ran hospitals and supplies for the army, and Lvov became the first head of the Provisional Government.

name: Cooperatives
sum: The consumers’ societies, led by moderate socialists, against the rising.

def.q: These were the workers’ and peasants’ Consumers’ Cooperative societies, which had several million members all over Russia before the Revolution.

background.en: Russia’s consumer, credit and producer cooperatives grew fast in the war and the revolution, with millions of members; their leaders, many of them Popular Socialists like Nikolai Tchaikovsky, sat in the Pre-Parliament and opposed the October rising.

name: Peasants’ Union
sum: The better-off peasants’ organisation, against the Peasants’ Soviets.

def.q: In 1917, however, it had become the political expression of the more prosperous peasants, to fight the growing power and revolutionary aims of the Soviets of Peasants’ Deputies.

background.en: The All-Russian Peasant Union was founded at a congress in Moscow in the summer of 1905 and demanded the land for those who work it and a constituent assembly. Revived in 1917, it was soon overtaken by the Soviets of Peasants’ Deputies.

name: Red Guards
sum: The armed workers of the factories: with the soldiers and sailors, they take the city and storm the Winter Palace.

def.q: The armed factory workers of Russia.

also.q: At every great crisis in the Revolution the Red Guards appeared on the streets, untrained and undisciplined, but full of Revolutionary zeal.

background.en: Workers’ militias formed in the factories after February 1917 and armed during General Kornilov’s attempt in August; by October Petrograd’s Red Guard numbered some twenty thousand men. They became the core of the Red Army, founded in 1918.

name: Stavka (General Headquarters)
sum: The army’s high command at Moghilev, far behind the front: after Kerensky flees it is the last centre of the old army, until Krylenko takes it in December.

def.q: Moghilev (General Staff Headquarters).

background.en: The Stavka, the headquarters of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief, stood at Moghilev from 1915. After the rising General Dukhonin, as acting Commander-in-Chief, refused the Soviet government’s order to open armistice talks; on 3 December 1917 Krylenko’s men took the Stavka and Dukhonin was killed.

name: Yunkers (officer cadets)
sum: The cadets of the military schools, the Government’s most dependable troops: they hold the Winter Palace on 7 November and rise against the Soviets on 11 November.

def.q: The yunkers of the Officers’ Schools of Pavlovsk, Tsarskoye Selo and Peterhof ordered by the Government to be ready to come to Petrograd.

also.q: In the Military Schools are retained only the arms necessary for instruction; all others are surrendered by the yunkers.

background.en: Yunkers were the cadets of Russia’s military schools, many of them sons of educated and propertied families. They were the Provisional Government’s most dependable troops: they defended the Winter Palace on 7 November and, on 11 November, rose against the Soviets in Petrograd at the call of the Committee for Salvation; many were killed when the Vladimir school was stormed.

name: Cossacks
sum: The cavalry of the Don and other borderlands: neutral in Petrograd, against the Soviets under Krasnov at Pulkovo and under Kaledin on the Don.

def.q: Now in the background of Russian politics began to form the vague outlines of a sinister power—the Cossacks.

background.en: The Cossacks were the military estates of the Don, the Kuban and other borderlands, who served as cavalry in return for land and self-government. In November 1917 the three Cossack regiments in Petrograd stayed neutral; General Krasnov’s Cossacks marched on the capital for Kerensky and were turned back at Pulkovo, and Ataman Kaledin raised the Don against the Soviets.

name: Death Battalions and the Women’s Battalion
sum: Volunteer shock units; women of the Petrograd battalion are among the Winter Palace’s defenders.

def.q: The Women’s Battalion is known to the world as the Death Battalion, but there were many Death Battalions composed of men.

background.en: Volunteer shock units raised in 1917 to stiffen the army by example. Maria Bochkareva’s 1st Russian Women’s Battalion of Death fought at the front in July 1917; a company of the 1st Petrograd Women’s Battalion was in the Winter Palace on 7 November.

name: White Guards
sum: Middle-class volunteers who take up arms for the old order.

def.q: Bourgeois volunteers, who emerged in the last stages of the Revolution, to defend private property from the Bolshevik attempt to abolish it.

background.en: The name passed to the anti-Bolshevik armies of the Civil War of 1918–1920, the Whites.

name: Tekhintsi and the “Savage Division”
sum: Kornilov’s own horsemen.

def.q: The so-called “Savage Division” in the army, made up of Mohametan tribesmen from Central Asia, and personally devoted to General Kornilov.

background.en: Kornilov’s personal guard was the Tekke regiment of Turkmen horsemen from Transcaspia; the “Savage Division”, the Caucasian Native Cavalry Division of volunteers from the North Caucasus, was part of the force he sent against Petrograd in August 1917, whose men were talked out of marching on by Soviet agitators.

name: Union of Officers
sum: The officers’ league against the soldiers’ committees.

def.q: An organisation formed among the reactionary officers in the army to combat politically the growing power of the Army Committees.

background.en: The Union of Officers of the Army and Navy, founded at Headquarters in May 1917, backed General Kornilov’s attempt in August 1917 and was suppressed after it failed.

name: Knights of St. George
sum: The holders of the Cross of St. George, for the war.

def.q: The Cross of St. George was awarded for distinguished action in battle.

background.en: The Cross of St George, the army’s highest award for bravery, was given to soldiers and officers; in 1917 its holders formed a union that backed the war and a firm government.
